Body Mapping: When and How

Purpose and scope

This guidance explains how staff complete a body map when they notice or are told about a mark, bruise or skin change on a resident. It applies to every care staff member.

Policy statement

A body map provides a clear, dated, consistent record of a mark's location, size and appearance, supporting both good skin care and, where relevant, a safeguarding referral, since a vague written description alone can be hard to compare accurately over time.

Definitions

**Body map** the standard diagram used to mark the exact location of a mark or injury on a resident's body. **Unexplained mark** a bruise, cut or skin change without an obvious, witnessed cause. **Baseline body map** the body map completed at admission, recording a resident's existing marks before any new one can be compared against it.

Roles and responsibilities

**Any care staff member** noticing a mark completes a body map the same shift, or reports it immediately to a colleague able to do so. **The registered manager** reviews an unexplained mark's body map to decide whether a safeguarding referral is needed. **New staff** are shown how to complete a body map correctly during induction.

1. Complete a body map for any new mark, bruise or skin change, marking its exact location, approximate size, and a brief description of its appearance.
2. Complete a baseline body map for every resident at admission, recording any existing mark before it could be mistaken for a new one later.
3. Take a photograph only where the resident consents and where photography is the site's approved method for the record, filed with the body map rather than kept separately.
4. Report an unexplained mark to the registered manager the same day, regardless of how minor it appears.

Worked example

A worked example illustrates baseline recording. A new resident is found to have an existing bruise on their forearm during admission. This is recorded on their baseline body map immediately, so that if a similar bruise is later noticed elsewhere, staff can clearly see it is a new, separate mark rather than mistakenly treating the original bruise as unexplained.

Frequently asked questions

**Does every mark need a safeguarding referral?** No, only one that is genuinely unexplained or gives cause for concern; a clearly explained, witnessed minor bump does not automatically require one, though it is still recorded. **Who can complete a body map?** Any care staff member trained at induction, not only a nurse or senior carer.

Training and competency

Body mapping is covered during safeguarding induction, with a practical demonstration of completing the diagram accurately.

Record keeping and retention

Completed body maps are retained in the resident's care record per the Records Retention Schedule.

Closing note

A clear, consistent body map protects a resident by making a genuine pattern visible over time, and this guidance exists to make that record easy to complete correctly under normal working conditions.

Duty of Candour: What Staff Need to Know

Purpose and scope

This guidance explains how Alderbridge Care Group meets its duty of candour when a notifiable safety incident occurs. It applies to every site and every member of staff involved in a resident's care.

Policy statement

Alderbridge is open and honest with a resident and their family when something has gone wrong in their care, explaining what happened, apologising genuinely, and setting out what will be done in response, because this openness is both a regulatory duty and simply the right thing to do.

Definitions

**Duty of candour** the statutory and professional duty to be open and transparent with a resident or their representative when a notifiable safety incident occurs. **Notifiable safety incident** an unintended or unexpected incident that resulted in, or could have resulted in, death or significant harm. **Reasonable apology** a genuine, meaningful apology for what happened, not a legal admission of liability.

Roles and responsibilities

**The registered manager** identifies whether an incident meets the notifiable threshold and leads the duty of candour conversation, or delegates this to a suitably senior colleague. **Care staff** report any incident that might meet the threshold promptly, without deciding themselves that it does not qualify. **The Quality Lead** supports the registered manager in preparing the written notification that follows the initial conversation.

Purpose and scope

This policy sets out how Alderbridge Care Group assesses falls risk and responds when a resident falls. It applies to every resident, with particular attention to a resident identified as being at higher risk.

Policy statement

Falls prevention balances a resident's right to move around freely with a proportionate response to their individual risk, since an overly restrictive approach can itself cause harm by reducing a resident's mobility, confidence and independence.

Definitions

Roles and responsibilities

Complete a falls risk assessment at admission and review it at least every three months, or sooner following any fall.

Following any fall, do not move the resident until a basic check for obvious injury has been completed, unless leaving them in place presents its own risk.

Contact the on-call registered manager immediately after any fall, regardless of whether an injury is apparent.

Statement. Race, religion or belief, sex, and sexual orientation are each protected in recruitment, employment and care delivery alike, and a resident's own view is never used to justify discriminatory treatment of a member of staff on any of these grounds, even where the resident's view reflects a genuinely held but discriminatory personal belief.

Handling a resident's discriminatory request in practice

Where a resident expresses a discriminatory preference about who provides their care, the registered manager discusses this sensitively with the resident directly, explaining Alderbridge's position, and considers whether the underlying need behind the request (for example, a genuine same-sex-carer preference for intimate personal care, which is a legitimate dignity consideration) can be met without discriminating against staff on a protected characteristic; where the request is simply discriminatory with no such legitimate underlying need, it is not accommodated, and the conversation with the resident and, where relevant, their family is recorded in their care plan so the position is consistent across every shift and every member of staff involved in their care.

Appendix: reasonable adjustments in recruitment

This appendix illustrates common reasonable adjustments made during Alderbridge recruitment, for hiring managers unfamiliar with the range of what might be requested. A candidate with dyslexia may be given extra time for a written exercise, or the option to complete it verbally instead, agreed in advance rather than raised as a surprise on the day. A candidate with a hearing impairment may be offered a British Sign Language interpreter or a written transcript of interview questions in advance. A candidate with a mobility impairment is offered step-free interview access at every Alderbridge site, confirmed in the invitation itself rather than left for the candidate to ask about. A candidate managing a mental health condition may request a shorter interview with scheduled breaks. None of these adjustments are treated as exceptional accommodations requiring special justification once genuinely requested — hiring managers are trained to expect and normalise such requests as an ordinary part of running a fair process.

Purpose and scope

This procedure sets out how Alderbridge Care Group prevents and responds to a slip, trip or fall hazard,
distinct from an individual resident's own falls risk assessment. It applies to every site.

Policy statement

A slip or trip hazard, such as a spillage or trailing cable, is addressed immediately on discovery, since
these hazards affect residents, staff and visitors alike and are often straightforward to remove once
noticed.

Definitions

**Immediate hazard** a spillage, obstruction or similar hazard requiring action the moment it is noticed.
**Wet floor sign** the visible warning sign placed at a wet or newly mopped area. **Hazard log** the record
of a recurring or structural hazard, such as uneven flooring, requiring a longer-term fix.

Roles and responsibilities

**Any staff member** noticing a spillage or obstruction addresses it immediately or arranges for it to be
addressed without delay. **Housekeeping** places a wet floor sign during any mopping or cleaning
activity. **Facilities** maintains the hazard log and arranges a longer-term fix for a structural issue.

1. Address a spillage or obstruction immediately on discovery, or arrange for it to be addressed without
delay if unable to do so personally.

2. Place a wet floor sign at any area being mopped or cleaned, removing it only once the floor is fully dry.

3. Report a recurring hazard, such as a loose carpet edge or uneven flooring, to facilities for the hazard
log, rather than only addressing each individual instance.

4. Keep a walkway clear of trailing cables, using an approved cable cover where a cable must temporarily
cross a walkway.

Exceptions and professional judgement

Where a hazard cannot be fully resolved immediately (for example, a spillage requiring specialist cleaning
equipment), the area is cordoned off and a wet floor sign placed while the fuller resolution is arranged,
rather than left unmarked in the meantime.

Hand Hygiene Policy

Purpose and scope

This policy sets out the hand hygiene standard expected of every member of staff at Alderbridge Care
Group. It applies to all care and non-care staff, and to anyone providing personal care to a resident.

Policy statement

Effective hand hygiene, performed at the right moments and using the right technique, is one of the single
most effective ways of preventing the spread of infection between residents, staff and visitors.

Definitions

**The Five Moments** the World Health Organization framework identifying the key points at which hand
hygiene must be performed: before touching a resident, before a clean or aseptic procedure, after a body
fluid exposure risk, after touching a resident, and after touching their surroundings. **Alcohol-based hand
rub** the primary method of hand hygiene where hands are not visibly soiled. **Bare below the elbows**
the standard requiring no wristwatch, jewellery (other than a plain band) or long sleeves during care
activity.

Roles and responsibilities

**All staff providing care** follow the Five Moments and bare-below-the-elbows standard during every shift.
**The Infection Prevention and Control Lead** audits hand hygiene compliance and technique across each
site. **The registered manager** ensures hand hygiene facilities and supplies are available and well
maintained at every point of care.

1. Perform hand hygiene at each of the Five Moments, using alcohol-based hand rub unless hands are
visibly soiled, in which case soap and water is used instead.

2. Follow the standard technique for the full recommended duration, covering all surfaces of the hand
including between fingers and thumbs.

3. Maintain bare-below-the-elbows during any care activity; a wristwatch, bracelet or long sleeve is
removed or rolled up before providing care.

4. Keep nails short and free of nail polish or false nails, since these can harbour bacteria and puncture a
glove.

Body Mapping: When and How

Purpose and scope

This guidance explains how staff complete a body map when they notice or are told about a mark, bruise or skin change on a resident. It applies to every care staff member.

Policy statement

A body map provides a clear, dated, consistent record of a mark's location, size and appearance, supporting both good skin care and, where relevant, a safeguarding referral, since a vague written description alone can be hard to compare accurately over time.

Definitions

**Body map** the standard diagram used to mark the exact location of a mark or injury on a resident's body. **Unexplained mark** a bruise, cut or skin change without an obvious, witnessed cause. **Baseline body map** the body map completed at admission, recording a resident's existing marks before any new one can be compared against it.

Roles and responsibilities

**Any care staff member** noticing a mark completes a body map the same shift, or reports it immediately to a colleague able to do so. **The registered manager** reviews an unexplained mark's body map to decide whether a safeguarding referral is needed. **New staff** are shown how to complete a body map correctly during induction.

1. Complete a body map for any new mark, bruise or skin change, marking its exact location, approximate size, and a brief description of its appearance.
2. Complete a baseline body map for every resident at admission, recording any existing mark before it could be mistaken for a new one later.
3. Take a photograph only where the resident consents and where photography is the site's approved method for the record, filed with the body map rather than kept separately.
4. Report an unexplained mark to the registered manager the same day, regardless of how minor it appears.

Frequently asked questions

Training and competency

Body mapping is covered during safeguarding induction, with a practical demonstration of completing the diagram accurately.

Record keeping and retention

Completed body maps are retained in the resident's care record per the Records Retention Schedule.

Closing note

A clear, consistent body map protects a resident by making a genuine pattern visible over time, and this guidance exists to make that record easy to complete correctly under normal working conditions.

Roles and responsibilities

**Every member of staff** has a personal, non-delegable duty to report a concern the same day,
regardless of seniority or how minor the concern initially appears. **The registered manager** is the site
safeguarding lead, responsible for making the LADO and local authority notification and for the immediate
safety of the person concerned. **The Alderbridge Safeguarding Lead** provides oversight across all five
sites, chairs the quarterly safeguarding review, and is the escalation point where a registered manager and
a family member disagree on the right course of action. **HR** leads any investigation where the person
alleged to have caused harm is a member of staff, working alongside, not instead of, the safeguarding
process.

1. If a person is in immediate danger, make them safe first — call 999 if needed — before doing anything
else.

2. Listen to what you are told without interrupting, without promising confidentiality you cannot keep, and
without asking leading questions that could compromise a later investigation.

3. Record exactly what was said, in the person's own words where possible, and exactly what you
observed, as soon as possible and always the same day.

4. Report the concern to the registered manager (or the on-call manager if out of hours) immediately —
never wait until the end of your shift.

5. Complete the Safeguarding Referral Form with the registered manager or under their direction.

6. The registered manager notifies the local authority safeguarding team and, where the concern involves
